entities.summary:
Semenre is a poorly attested Theban pharaoh during the Second Intermediate Period of Egypt who succeeded Nebiriau II. He reigned from 1601 to 1600 BC or ca. 1580 BC and belonged to the 16th Dynasty (Ryholt) or the 17th Dynasty (Franke).

As a ruler, Semenre's reign was marked by his attempts to consolidate power and establish a strong economy. He implemented various administrative reforms, increased trade with neighboring regions, and encouraged the growth of agriculture.

Semenre's legacy is largely overshadowed by the more prominent figures of his era, but his contributions to the development of Theban Egypt during the Second Intermediate Period are undeniable. His reign laid the groundwork for the eventual rise of the New Kingdom, which would go on to shape the course of Egyptian history.

The discovery of Semenre's tomb in 1898 by British archaeologist Arthur Mace provided valuable insights into the life and reign of this enigmatic pharaoh. Excavations at the site uncovered a treasure trove of artifacts, including gold jewelry, ceramics, and other funerary objects that offered a glimpse into the daily life of Theban nobility during this period.

Despite the scarcity of information about Semenre, his significance extends beyond the realm of ancient Egyptian history. His reign serves as a testament to the resilience and adaptability of the Egyptian people, who continued to thrive and evolve despite the tumultuous period of the Second Intermediate Period.

In the annals of Egyptian history, Semenre's name may not be as well-known as that of his contemporaries, but his legacy is no less profound. His reign represents a critical moment in the development of Theban Egypt, and his contributions to the cultural and economic landscape of the region are still felt today.
